questions.stem: Benning's year-end bonus from Global is based on the level of her clients' participation in IPOs, and she does not disclose the arrangement to those clients. Benning's failure to disclose is most likely:

options.A: a violation of Standard IV(B), as the bonus is additional compensation requiring consent.
options.B: a violation of Standard VI(A), as her stake competes with her clients' interests.
options.C: not a violation, as the bonus is set and paid by her own employer, Global.

rationales.A: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements addresses gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration received from outside parties that compete with or might create a conflict with the employer's interest, and it is satisfied by written consent from all parties involved. This bonus is paid by the employer itself, so no outside party is involved and IV(B) is not the operative standard. The disclosable conflict runs to the clients and falls under Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts.
rationales.B: Benning's year-end bonus is based on the level of her clients' participation in IPOs, which creates a conflict of interest between Benning and her clients: is she recommending IPOs to clients based on their best interest or on hers? By not disclosing the arrangement, Benning is in violation of Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts, which requires full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair her independence and objectivity or interfere with her duties to clients. Global can avoid this conflict by not compensating Benning in this way.
rationales.C: A bonus tied to the level of her clients' IPO participation creates a conflict of interest between Benning and her clients, since it gives her a personal stake in how much of the firm's new issues they buy. Standard VI(A) requires such conflicts to be avoided or disclosed to clients, and the fact that her own employer sets and pays the bonus does not make it a purely internal matter. Global can avoid the conflict by not compensating her in this way.

questions.stem: Benning allocates FTSX IPO shares only to those institutional clients who commit to purchasing additional shares in the secondary market once the stock begins trading. Benning's allocation is most likely:

options.A: a violation of Standards II(B) and III(B), as this is a tie-in agreement.
options.B: not a violation, as the clients who wanted more shares were treated fairly.
options.C: not a violation, as Benning followed her employer's allocation policy.

rationales.A: This is an example of a tie-in agreement, in which the underwriter requires the investor to buy more shares of a new issue in the secondary market as a condition of buying shares in the IPO. The purpose and effect of such an arrangement is to artificially increase demand and support a higher share price once trading begins. Tie-in agreements violate Standard II(B) Market Manipulation, under which members must not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants. The practice also violates Standard III(B) Fair Dealing, because Benning is not treating all of her institutional clients fairly: she is allocating IPO shares only to those clients who agree to purchase additional shares once FTSX begins trading.
rationales.B: Conditioning an IPO allocation on a commitment to buy more shares in the secondary market is a tie-in agreement, whose purpose and effect is to artificially increase demand and support a higher share price, which distorts prices and inflates trading volume in violation of Standard II(B) Market Manipulation. It also breaches Standard III(B) Fair Dealing, because the institutional clients who did not agree to the secondary purchases were shut out of the allocation, so the clients were not all dealt with fairly.
rationales.C: An employer's allocation policy cannot authorize a tie-in scheme that inflates aftermarket demand; the Code and Standards are the governing obligation. Tie-in agreements violate Standard II(B) Market Manipulation, which prohibits practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants, and the selective allocation to clients who agree to buy more shares also violates Standard III(B) Fair Dealing.

questions.stem: After Deacon signed the Option Account Application and Agreement, Benning changes the language on the form pertaining to Deacon's suitability for options and initials the change on Deacon's behalf. Benning's action is most likely:

options.A: a violation of Standard I(D), as initialing for the client is deceit.
options.B: not a violation, as the change to the suitability language was immaterial.
options.C: not a violation, as Benning acted to spare Deacon a second trip to the office.

rationales.A: By changing the language on the Option Account Application and Agreement and initialing the form on behalf of Deacon, Benning is in violation of Standard I(D) Misconduct, under which members and candidates must not engage in any professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit or commit any act that reflects adversely on their professional reputation, integrity, or competence. Initialing a client's document in the client's place misrepresents to everyone who later reads the form that Deacon approved the amended language. Even a change Benning believed to be in Deacon's best interests cannot be effected without Deacon's own written approval.
rationales.B: Materiality is no defense. Altering a client document after the client has signed it, and initialing the alteration on her behalf, is conduct involving dishonesty and deceit under Standard I(D) Misconduct and reflects adversely on Benning's professional integrity. Suitability language on an options account agreement is in any case central to the document, and even changes Benning believed to be in Deacon's best interest cannot be effected without Deacon's own written approval.
rationales.C: Altering a signed suitability document and initialing it on the client's behalf involves dishonesty and deceit under Standard I(D) Misconduct, and sparing the client an errand is no defense. Benning could have obtained Deacon's own initials, since a change to a document the client has already signed cannot be effected without Deacon's written approval.

questions.stem: Benning's client Deacon approves an Account Linking form during a telephone call, after which Benning signs the form on Deacon's behalf. Benning's conduct is most likely:

options.A: a violation of Standard I(D) Misconduct.
options.B: a violation of Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care.
options.C: not a violation of the Code and Standards.

rationales.A: Signing the Account Linking form on behalf of Deacon is a violation of Standard I(D) Misconduct. The approval Benning received over the telephone to sign the form is insufficient: Benning needs Deacon to personally sign the authorization. Standard I(D) covers conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit, and executing a client's signature oneself is deceitful regardless of the adviser's good intentions or of the client's oral agreement with the substance of the transaction.
rationales.B: This misattributes the conduct to the duty of care. Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care governs the care, skill, and diligence with which a member acts for a client; the defect here is not imprudent management of Deacon's assets but the deceit of signing a form in the client's name. That conduct is professional misconduct under Standard I(D), and the remedy is to have Deacon personally sign the authorization rather than to raise the standard of care applied to her account.
rationales.C: This reflects the misconception that oral consent suffices. The approval Benning received over the telephone to sign the Account Linking form is insufficient, because Standard I(D) requires Deacon to personally sign the authorization. A telephone approval may establish that Deacon wanted the accounts linked, but it does not permit Benning to execute Deacon's signature for her, so the violation stands.

questions.stem: Steve Deacon tells Benning that his wife, Benning's client and the sole holder of her account, has serious health issues, and he requests a $15,000 redemption. Over the following weeks Benning completes several redemptions and withdrawals at Steve's request. Benning's conduct is most likely:

options.A: no violation of Standard III(A), given the medical emergency.
options.B: no violation of Standard III(A), given spousal authority.
options.C: a violation of Standard III(A), given the lack of authorization.

rationales.A: Sympathy does not create authority. A family medical emergency may explain why Benning acted quickly, but Deacon, the account holder, gave no authorization for her husband to direct transactions in her account, and urgency is not a substitute for that authorization. Even if Benning was acting in what she believed to be Deacon's best interests, transacting at the husband's request without Deacon's authorization violates Standard III(A).
rationales.B: No such presumption exists. The account is individually held by Deacon, and Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care requires actual authority or authorization from the account holder before a member acts on any third party's instructions, spouse or not. Marriage does not confer trading authority over an individually held account; a power of attorney or the account holder's own written authorization would.
rationales.C: By redeeming shares and processing withdrawals in Deacon's account at her husband's request, Benning is in violation of Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care. Benning has no authority or authorization from Deacon, the account holder, allowing Deacon's husband, Steve, to redeem shares and approve withdrawals from her account. Even if Benning was acting in Deacon's best interests, transacting at the husband's request without Deacon's authorization violates the Standards.

questions.stem: Hill's marketing material states that his fund is the best-performing fund in Australian equities over the past 10-year period and that it delivered a return of 28.7%, gross of fees, over the past one-year period. Hill's statement is most likely:

options.A: a violation of Standard III(D) Performance Presentation.
options.B: a violation of Standard I(C) Misrepresentation.
options.C: not a violation of the Code and Standards.

rationales.A: Standard III(D) Performance Presentation does not mandate net-of-fees presentation. Members and candidates can meet their obligations under Standard III(D) by including disclosures that fully explain the performance results being reported: for example, stating when appropriate that results are simulated when model results are used, clearly indicating when the performance record is that of a prior entity, or disclosing whether the performance is gross of fees, net of fees, or after tax. Hill explicitly states that the 28.7% return is gross of fees, or pre-fees, so the obligation is met through disclosure.
rationales.B: There is no evidence that Hill's statements are false or opinion based. In speaking about the fund's performance he is stating facts: the fund's 10-year record and its one-year return, with the fee basis disclosed. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation addresses knowingly making untrue statements or omissions relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities, and an accurate performance figure presented with its fee basis is not such a statement.
rationales.C: There is no violation, because Hill states that the performance is gross of fees, or pre-fees. Under the guidance to Standard III(D) Performance Presentation, members and candidates can meet their obligations by including disclosures that fully explain the performance results being reported, for example by disclosing whether the performance is gross of fees, net of fees, or after tax. Hill's statements about the fund's 10-year record and its 28.7% one-year return are statements of fact rather than false or opinion-based claims, so neither Standard III(D) nor Standard I(C) is breached.

questions.stem: Hill accepts thank-you gift bags containing wine, retail gift cards, restaurant certificates, and travel discounts from the sponsors of talk shows on which he appears, and he does not disclose them to his employer. Hill's acceptance of the gift bags is most likely:

options.A: a violation of Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements.
options.B: a violation of Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity.
options.C: not a violation of the Code and Standards.

rationales.A: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements is triggered by gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with, or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with, the employer's interest; only then is written consent from all parties required. Ordinary thank-you gift bags from the sponsors of the shows on which Hill appears create no such conflict with the interests of his employer or of the fund, so no written consent was needed and the Standard is not engaged.
rationales.B: Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity requires members to use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity, and not to accept any gift or benefit that could reasonably be expected to compromise their own or another's independence. Wine, retail gift cards, restaurant certificates, and travel discounts given to a guest by talk-show sponsors are modest tokens unrelated to any investment recommendation, and nothing about them reasonably compromises Hill's investment independence.
rationales.C: There is no violation. Under Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements, members and candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved. Hill's appearance on these shows does not create a conflict of interest with the interests of his employer or of the fund, so the gift bags fall outside the Standard and the absence of disclosure to the employer is not itself a breach.

questions.stem: While still employed at their current firm, Hill and 10 team members use time outside of work and on weekends to lease office space for a new firm and to register individually with government authorities. Their conduct is most likely:

options.A: no violation of Standard IV(A), given the use of personal time.
options.B: a violation of Standard IV(A), given the preparations to compete.
options.C: a violation of Standard IV(A), given the registrations.

rationales.A: There is no violation. Hill and the individuals joining him at the new firm are making preparations outside of work and on weekends, using that time to lease office space and to register individually with government authorities. Their actions to start a new business do not occur during hours when their employer would expect them to be at work, so they are not using work time and are not breaching their duty of loyalty under Standard IV(A).
rationales.B: Standard IV(A) Loyalty does not prohibit preparations to start a new business. Members may make arrangements to go into a competing business provided those arrangements do not interfere with the current employer's business and do not use the employer's time, property, or resources. Because Hill and the individuals joining him used time outside of work and on weekends to lease office space and to register, they were not using hours their employer expected them to be at work and did not breach their duty of loyalty.
rationales.C: Registering individually with government authorities is permissible preparation, not solicitation of the employer's clients or business. Standard IV(A) Loyalty is concerned with misappropriating the employer's clients, records, or trade secrets and with competing with the employer while using its time or resources; obtaining one's own registrations takes nothing from the employer and solicits none of its clients. Conducted outside working hours, it does not breach Standard IV(A).

questions.stem: Hill's team is subject to no noncompete agreement, and Hill tells the team that they can begin soliciting former clients on the day their new firm opens. Hill's instruction is most likely:

options.A: not a violation of the Code and Standards.
options.B: a violation of Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors.
options.C: a violation of Standard IV(A) Loyalty.

rationales.A: There is no violation. Under the guidance to Standard IV(A) Loyalty, once employment with the former firm has ended, the Standard does not prohibit members and candidates from contacting clients of their previous firm, as long as the contact information does not come from the records of, or as a result of work for, the former employer, and as long as such outreach does not violate an applicable agreement. By telling his team to begin solicitation after they have left the fund and on the new firm's opening day, not prior to its opening, and given that there is no noncompete agreement, Hill is not in violation.
rationales.B: Directing lawful post-departure solicitation is not a supervision failure. Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires those with supervisory responsibility to make reasonable efforts to detect and prevent violations of applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards. Because the solicitation Hill directs is itself permitted, occurring after the team has left and with no noncompete agreement in force, there is no violation for him to have detected or prevented.
rationales.C: Standard IV(A) Loyalty governs the employment relationship: it bars competing with the employer while still employed, using the employer's time, property, or records, and soliciting the employer's clients before departure. The solicitation Hill directs begins on the new firm's opening day, after the team has left, uses contact information obtained independently of former-firm records, and runs against no noncompete agreement, so Standard IV(A) does not reach it. Nor do the Code and Standards impose any cooling-off period after departure during which former clients may not be contacted.

questions.stem: Portman invites Hill to important client meetings and discusses Hill's stock-picking acumen, and he refers client questions to Martin, whom he describes as Hill's assistant, although Martin has been making the investment decisions. Portman's conduct is most likely:

options.A: a violation of Standard I(C) regarding the fund's strategy.
options.B: a violation of Standard I(C) regarding decision making.
options.C: no violation of Standard I(C) Misrepresentation.

rationales.A: The misrepresentation concerns roles and responsibilities, not the strategy. Nothing in Portman's conduct misstates how the fund invests; what he misstates is who does the investing. The Standard cited is the right one, but the subject of the misstatement identified here does not match the facts: the impression created is about which individual is responsible for stock selection and investment decision making.
rationales.B: By inviting Hill to client meetings, discussing Hill's stock-picking acumen, and referring to Martin as Hill's assistant, Portman is giving clients the impression that Hill is responsible for stock selection and investment decision making at the fund, when Martin has actually been making those decisions. Portman is therefore in violation of Standard I(C) Misrepresentation: members and candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities.
rationales.C: Presenting senior colleagues favorably is ordinary sales practice, but creating the impression that Hill is responsible for stock selection and investment decision making while the person actually making those decisions is cast as his assistant misrepresents who does what at the fund. That goes beyond puffery and is a knowing misrepresentation relating to investment actions and other professional activities under Standard I(C).

questions.stem: A fund's chief investment officer and two of its board members sell their shares in the fund and in its management company before the public announcement that the fund's lead portfolio manager is resigning. Their sale of the shares is most likely:

options.A: a violation of Standard II(A), given the undisclosed resignation.
options.B: no violation of Standard II(A), given insiders' trading rights.
options.C: no violation of Standard II(A), given the immateriality.

rationales.A: By selling their shares before the lead portfolio manager's resignation was announced, the chief investment officer and the two board members acted on material nonpublic information. Under Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information, members and candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information. Information is material if its disclosure would probably have an impact on the price of a security, or if reasonable investors would want to know the information before making an investment decision, and the undisclosed departure of the fund's lead portfolio manager meets that test.
rationales.B: Insider status heightens rather than removes the prohibition on trading on material nonpublic information. Standard II(A) applies to any member or candidate who possesses material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment, whatever their position and whatever the origin of the shares sold, and these officers sold on undisclosed information about the lead portfolio manager's resignation before it was announced publicly.
rationales.C: The departure of a fund's lead portfolio manager is plainly material to the fund and to its management company: its disclosure would probably have an impact on the price of those shares, and reasonable investors would want to know it before making an investment decision. Selling before the announcement is therefore acting on material nonpublic information under Standard II(A).

questions.stem: Portman has heard rumors that his fund's lead portfolio manager is resigning but does not know whether the manager will do so. After a business news channel reports that the fund's chief investment officer and two board members have sold their shares in the fund's management company, Portman sells his own shares in that company. Portman's sale is most likely:

options.A: no violation of Standard II(A), given the public report.
options.B: a violation of Standard II(A), given the resignation rumors.
options.C: a violation of Standard II(A), given the timing of the sale.

rationales.A: There is no violation. Portman does not know definitively whether the lead portfolio manager is resigning. In addition to the rumors he heard, his sell decision is based on learning from the business news channel that the chief investment officer and two board members sold their shares. Portman's decision to sell is not based on material nonpublic information, because this information was publicly reported, so he is not in violation of Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information.
rationales.B: Portman does not know definitively whether the lead portfolio manager is resigning, so unconfirmed rumors are not material nonpublic information in his possession. His sell decision rests on learning of the chief investment officer's and the board members' sales from the business news channel, which is publicly reported information, and acting on publicly disseminated information is not acting on material nonpublic information under Standard II(A).
rationales.C: The officers' share sales were publicly reported on the business news channel. Once information has been publicly disseminated, Standard II(A) imposes no additional waiting period before members may act on it: the prohibition reaches information that is both material and nonpublic, and this information was public when Portman traded.

questions.stem: Graeme receives commissions on the new issues he recommends. His firm's policy does not require disclosure of those commissions because clients receive prospectuses, and Graeme discloses them only to clients who ask. Graeme's practice is most likely:

options.A: no violation of Standard VI(A), given the prospectuses.
options.B: no violation of Standard VI(A), given the firm's policy.
options.C: a violation of Standard VI(A), given the partial disclosure.

rationales.A: Prospectus delivery is not effective, prominent disclosure of Graeme's own conflict. Standard VI(A) requires full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair independence and objectivity, made in plain language and in a manner effective in communicating the information to clients. Graeme can avoid the conflict by not accepting the commissions; if he does not, he must inform all clients of the commissions he receives on new issues, regardless of what appears in the prospectuses.
rationales.B: Firm policy cannot narrow Standard VI(A). The member's obligation runs to clients under the Code and Standards, and where the employer's policy is less demanding, the Standard governs. If Graeme does not avoid the conflict by declining the commissions, he must inform all clients, not just those who ask, of the commissions he receives on new issues, so that his clients have the information necessary to evaluate the objectivity of his advice, regardless of his firm's policy.
rationales.C: Graeme is in violation of Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts. He can avoid the conflict by not accepting commissions from new issues. If he does not avoid the conflict, Graeme must inform all clients, not just those who ask, of the commissions he receives on new issues, so that his clients have the information necessary to evaluate the objectivity of the investment advice or action taken by him on their behalf. The Standard requires this regardless of his firm's disclosure policy and regardless of what appears in the prospectuses clients receive.

questions.stem: The Delaneys have a 15- to 20-year time horizon and a low risk tolerance, and they are unwilling to accept high levels of volatility. The majority of Graeme's purchases for their account were new issues, and his longest holding period was five months. Graeme's conduct most likely violates:

options.A: No Standard.
options.B: Standard III(C) Suitability.
options.C: Standard III(D) Performance Presentation.

rationales.A: Graeme's trading did breach a standard. The Delaneys' stated risk tolerance is low and their time horizon is 15 to 20 years, yet the majority of the purchases in their account were new issues held for less than five months. That is a pattern of short-horizon, high-volatility trading, and Standard III(C) Suitability does not permit it in an account carrying those objectives and constraints.
rationales.B: Standard III(C) Suitability requires a member in an advisory relationship to determine that an investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints. The Delaneys stated that their risk tolerance is low, which means they were unwilling to accept high levels of volatility in their portfolio. By purchasing new issues in their account and holding them for less than five months, Graeme took on volatility that is unsuitable for that risk tolerance and inconsistent with a 15- to 20-year horizon, so he violated Standard III(C).
rationales.C: The defect is the unsuitability of the portfolio under Standard III(C). Nothing in the facts involves reporting or presenting investment performance, which is the domain of Standard III(D); Graeme's trading simply conflicted with the Delaneys' low risk tolerance and long time horizon.

questions.stem: Balmer raised her concerns about Graeme's use of new issues with him during her end-of-year meeting and then reported those concerns to BOA's director of compliance. With respect to the Code and Standards, Balmer most likely:

options.A: Did not violate the Code and Standards.
options.B: Violated Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors.
options.C: Violated Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law.

rationales.A: Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires members with supervisory responsibility to make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards. Balmer raised her concerns with Graeme directly at her end-of-year meeting and then escalated those concerns by reporting them to BOA's director of compliance. Both steps are what is required of a supervisor, so Balmer did not violate the Code and Standards.
rationales.B: This reflects the misconception that a supervisor is liable for any violation committed by a subordinate. Standard IV(C) calls for reasonable efforts to detect and prevent violations rather than a guarantee of compliance, and Balmer met that standard by raising her concerns with Graeme and escalating them to the director of compliance.
rationales.C: Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law requires members to know and comply with applicable laws, rules, and regulations and the Code and Standards, and to dissociate from any violation. It does not compel a member to report a colleague's conduct to a securities regulator in the absence of a legal requirement to do so. Internal escalation to the firm's compliance department is the appropriate response, and that is what Balmer did, so she did not violate Standard I(A).

questions.stem: Graeme has never updated Milgram's investment policy statement since it was first put in place five years ago. Graeme's conduct most likely violates:

options.A: Standard III(C) Suitability.
options.B: Standard V(C) Record Retention.
options.C: No Standard.

rationales.A: Standard III(C) Suitability requires a member in an advisory relationship to gather information about the client's financial situation, investment experience, and objectives, and to reassess and update that information regularly. Graeme has not updated Milgram's investment policy statement since it was first put in place, which places him in violation of Standard III(C).
rationales.B: Standard V(C) Record Retention governs the records a member keeps to support investment analyses, recommendations, and actions. The failure here is not one of recordkeeping but of maintaining current suitability information, so the operative standard is III(C), not V(C).
rationales.C: This reflects the misconception that suitability is a one-time step taken at the inception of the relationship. Standard III(C) requires members to reassess and update client information regularly, whether or not the client asks for a review.

questions.stem: When Milgram complained, Balmer called Graeme into her office and sat in on the meeting in which Graeme reviewed Milgram's account and investment policy statement. With respect to Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors, Balmer most likely:

options.A: Violated it by not escalating the complaint to the board.
options.B: Violated it by not restricting Graeme's activities.
options.C: Satisfied it by investigating the complaint.

rationales.A: Standard IV(C) requires a supervisor who learns that an employee may have violated the law or the Code and Standards to promptly initiate an assessment of the extent of the wrongdoing. Calling Graeme into her office and sitting in on the review of the account and the investment policy statement is that prompt assessment; immediate escalation to the board is not the required first step.
rationales.B: Standard IV(C) requires the supervisor to promptly initiate an assessment of the possible wrongdoing, which Balmer did by calling Graeme into her office and sitting in on the review of Milgram's account and investment policy statement. Restricting an employee's activities is a response reserved for wrongdoing that is ongoing or likely to continue; it is not a prerequisite of every inquiry.
rationales.C: As soon as she was made aware of the complaint, Balmer initiated an investigation by calling Graeme into her office, and she sat in on the meeting in which he reviewed Milgram's account and investment policy statement. Under Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors, once a supervisor learns that an employee has violated or may have violated the law or the Code and Standards, the supervisor must promptly initiate an assessment to determine the extent of the wrongdoing; relying on the employee's statements about the extent of the violation, or on assurances that the wrongdoing will not reoccur, is not enough. Balmer's active investigation meets that requirement, so she did not violate the Code and Standards.

questions.stem: Yousoff and Wong agree to pay Tan and Chuong, two board members who built the relationship with MGM2, a portion of the advisory fees MGM2 pays, and the arrangement is not disclosed in the memorandum of understanding. The arrangement most likely:

options.A: Violates Standard VI(C) Referral Fees.
options.B: Violates no Standard.
options.C: Violates Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts.

rationales.A: A referral fee is compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services. Tan and Chuong did not refer MGM2 to GHB; they worked to bring MGM2 on as a client, and the payment compensates that business-development effort rather than a recommendation, so Standard VI(C) is not engaged.
rationales.B: The fee-sharing arrangement is a reward paid to Tan and Chuong for their efforts to bring MGM2 on as a client, not a referral fee. Tan and Chuong did not refer MGM2 to GHB, and a referral fee is compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services. The facts also provide no evidence that a conflict of interest is present, so Yousoff is not in violation of the Code and Standards.
rationales.C: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts addresses relationships and interests that could reasonably be expected to impair a member's independence and objectivity. As structured, the payment is legitimate compensation for work done to win the mandate, and the facts provide no evidence that a conflict of interest is present, so no violation arises from the memorandum of understanding itself.

questions.stem: Hie, who helped found MGM2, recently hired the son of GHB board member Chuong into an executive role at Hie's firm, and Chuong does not tell Yousoff. Chuong's silence most likely violates:

options.A: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation.
options.B: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts.
options.C: No Standard.

rationales.A: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation covers untrue statements and omissions that misstate facts about services, qualifications, or performance. Chuong's silence is an undisclosed conflict of interest rather than an affirmative misrepresentation of that kind, so I(C) is not the operative standard.
rationales.B: Hie's hiring of Chuong's son in an executive position at Hie's firm could reasonably be expected to impair Chuong's independence and objectivity with respect to interactions between MGM2 and GHB. Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts requires members to make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity, and it therefore requires Chuong to disclose this conflict.
rationales.C: The son's employment is not a purely private matter for disclosure purposes. Hie hiring him into an executive role could reasonably be expected to impair Chuong's objectivity toward Hie's business, which makes it a conflict that Standard VI(A) requires Chuong to disclose.

questions.stem: Sim uses a fact sheet Hie provided to prepare his investment policy statement and, at Hie's request, destroys the other notes she took during their meeting. Destroying those notes is most likely:

options.A: Permitted, as her notes duplicate Hie's fact sheet.
options.B: Permitted, as Hie requested confidentiality.
options.C: Prohibited, as the notes are records she must retain.

rationales.A: Her notes are not duplicative working papers. The guidance for Standard V(C) states that members must retain records that substantiate the scope of their research and the reasons for their actions or conclusions, and it lists notes from clients among the examples of supporting documentation, so the fact sheet does not stand in for them. By destroying all her notes from the meeting, Sim fails to maintain appropriate records to support her investment actions.
rationales.B: A duty of confidentiality protects client information from disclosure to outsiders; it does not authorize destroying the records that support the investment policy statement and the advice given. Sim could have retained the notes and kept them confidential, so the client's request does not excuse the failure to maintain appropriate records.
rationales.C: Standard V(C) Record Retention requires members and candidates to develop and maintain appropriate records to support their investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and other investment-related communications with clients and prospective clients. The guidance adds that members must retain records that substantiate the scope of their research and the reasons for their actions or conclusions, and some examples of supporting documentation include notes from clients. By destroying all notes from their meeting, Sim is not maintaining appropriate records to support her investment actions, which violates Standard V(C).

questions.stem: Hie promises Sim a bonus at year-end if she processes his transactions in a timely manner, and Sim does not tell Yousoff, her employer, about the promise. Sim's conduct most likely violates:

options.A: Standard IV(B), which requires written consent from all parties involved.
options.B: Standard VI(A), which requires prominent disclosure to all her other clients.
options.C: No Standard, since a bonus from a grateful client is a personal gift.

rationales.A: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements provides that members and candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with, or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with, their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved. Hie's promise of a bonus if Sim processes his transactions in a timely manner could conflict with Sim's responsibilities to her other clients or to other clients of GHB. At a minimum, Sim must disclose the bonus arrangement to Yousoff, her employer, and by not doing so she violated the Code and Standards.
rationales.B: Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts does reach an arrangement of this kind, but what it calls for is full and fair disclosure to the parties whose interests the conflict touches, which here means Sim's employer. It does not call for the prominent disclosure to all of her other clients that this option prescribes. The operative failure is the undisclosed additional-compensation arrangement with a client that competes with her employer's interest, and Standard IV(B) addresses that directly by requiring written consent from all parties involved.
rationales.C: A payment promised by a client does not fall outside the standard merely because the client is grateful. A year-end bonus contingent on the timeliness with which Sim processes that client's transactions is consideration that might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with her employer's interest, so Standard IV(B) requires written consent from all parties involved before she accepts it.

questions.stem: Hie refuses to answer Sim's questions about his risk tolerance, objectives, and investment experience, saying that he will initially invest only in short-term US government securities, and Sim opens the account using the fact sheet he provided. Opening the account is most likely:

options.A: Permitted, as short-term government securities are riskless.
options.B: Prohibited, as the required client information was not gathered.
options.C: Permitted, as Hie waived the suitability inquiry.

rationales.A: Suitability information, meaning the client's investment experience, objectives, and risk tolerance, must be gathered at the inception of an advisory relationship regardless of how safe the client's intended initial holdings appear. The advisory relationship and the investment policy statement extend well beyond those first holdings, so the low risk of short-term government securities does not excuse the omission.
rationales.B: Standard III(C) Suitability requires that, when an advisory relationship exists, members and candidates must gather client information at the inception of the relationship. Sim did not complete the required section on Hie's investment experience, objectives, and risk tolerance of new clients, and the information Hie provided was not sufficient for Sim to develop an appropriate investment policy statement. A client's statement regarding his or her desired investment strategy, especially without a fully formed investment policy statement, does not meet the requirements of III(C), so Sim violated Standard III(C).
rationales.C: A client cannot waive the inception inquiry. Standard III(C) requires members in an advisory relationship to gather information on the client's investment experience, objectives, and risk tolerance at the inception of the relationship, and Hie's fact sheet was not sufficient for Sim to develop an appropriate investment policy statement.

questions.stem: Sim believes that Hie may be using his account to launder money, and Yousoff, her supervisor, dismisses her concerns. Sim's most appropriate first course of action is to:

options.A: take no further action.
options.B: contact the regulator in her jurisdiction.
options.C: contact her firm's compliance department.

rationales.A: Having informed Yousoff is not sufficient once he has dismissed the concern. A member who suspects that a client may be using an account to launder money must not knowingly participate in or assist the suspected activity, and doing nothing further leaves her associated with it.
rationales.B: Approaching the regulator is not the first step. The guidance for Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law directs a member who is in doubt about the appropriate action to seek the advice of compliance personnel or legal counsel first; recourse outside the firm may follow if the firm fails to act, but it does not lead.
rationales.C: The guidance for Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law states that when in doubt about the appropriate action to undertake, it is recommended that a member or candidate seek the advice of compliance personnel or legal counsel concerning legal requirements, and that if a potential violation is being committed by a fellow employee, it may also be prudent for the member or candidate to seek the advice of the firm's compliance department or legal counsel. With Yousoff having dismissed her concerns, Sim's appropriate first course of action is to take her concerns to her firm's compliance department.

questions.stem: Madam Tan, age 70 and retired, holds fixed deposits and lower-risk energy utility shares and wants to add conservative equities to fund her grandchildren's education. After friends mention an oil-linked structured note, she asks her adviser, Sim, about it. Sim summarizes the note's features and risks verbally, and Madam Tan then says she is unsure what oil futures are or how they work but directs that $50,000 be invested in the note. Sim's acceptance of the order is most likely:

options.A: impermissible, because the note is unsuitable for her.
options.B: permissible, because the request was hers and unsolicited.
options.C: permissible, because Sim summarized the note's risks.

rationales.A: Madam Tan is 70 and retired, holds fixed deposits and lower-risk energy utility shares, and now wants to add conservative equities to fund her grandchildren's education. An oil-linked structured note is not a conservative equity investment, and she tells Sim she is unsure what oil futures are or how they work. Standard III(C) Suitability requires a member to judge an investment against the client's objectives, constraints, and risk tolerance as set out in the agreed-on investment policy statement, and members and candidates need to make reasonable efforts to balance clients' trading requests with their responsibility to follow that statement. Accepting the $50,000 order violates Standard III(C).
rationales.B: A client-initiated, unsolicited request does not transfer the suitability obligation to the client. Members and candidates still need to make reasonable efforts to balance clients' trading requests with their responsibility to follow the agreed-on investment policy statement. Madam Tan's conservative objectives and low risk tolerance make the structured note unsuitable for her portfolio, so Standard III(C) Suitability is violated whatever the origin of the request.
rationales.C: A verbal summary of features and risks does not cure unsuitability; disclosure is not a substitute for a suitability judgment. The summary plainly did not inform her, because she goes on to say she is unsure what oil futures are or how they work. Since the note conflicts with her stated wish to invest in conservative equities, Sim still violates Standard III(C) Suitability by accepting the order.

questions.stem: Hie, a client of Sim, has told her to seek information as needed from board members Tan and Chuong. Sim's discussion of Hie's account with Tan and Chuong is most likely:

options.A: permissible, because the client waived confidentiality.
options.B: impermissible, because board members are third parties.
options.C: impermissible, because the waiver was not in writing.

rationales.A: Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality requires members to keep information about current, former, and prospective clients confidential, but a member or candidate can break that confidence when permission is granted by the client. Hie granted that permission when he told Sim to seek information as needed from board members Tan and Chuong, so her discussion of his account with them falls within what he authorized and she is not in violation of the Code and Standards.
rationales.B: Third-party status is not the test. Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality bars disclosure to outsiders only where the client has not authorized it, and client-authorized sharing is a recognized exception to the duty. Hie told Sim to seek information as needed from the two board members, so discussing the account with Tan and Chuong is not a breach of confidentiality.
rationales.C: Standard III(E) turns on whether the client granted permission, not on the form that permission took. Hie's instruction to seek information as needed from board members Tan and Chuong is itself a grant of permission; no written documentation is required before Sim may rely on it, so she is not in violation.

questions.stem: The ethical decision-making framework most likely concludes with:

options.A: a review of whether the outcome was as anticipated.
options.B: a compliance review opened once a violation is suspected.
options.C: the decision and the action that implements it.

rationales.A: The framework has four components. Identify: relevant facts, stakeholders and duties owed, ethical principles, and conflicts of interest. Consider: situational influences, additional guidance, and alternative actions. Decide and act. Reflect: was the outcome as anticipated, and why or why not? The components do not need to be addressed in the sequence shown, but a review of the outcome should conclude the process, because that review provides insights for improved decision making in the future.
rationales.B: The framework is a prospective decision aid, not a post hoc audit tool. Identify, consider, decide and act, and reflect are meant to be worked through as a decision is being made, with the reflection step closing the loop afterward so that later decisions improve. A review opened only once a violation is suspected is a compliance investigation rather than the component that concludes the framework, and treating the framework that way would leave the identify and consider components with nothing to do.
rationales.C: Deciding and acting is not the last component. Although the framework's components do not need to be addressed in the sequence shown, a review of the outcome should conclude the process: reflect asks whether the outcome was as anticipated, and why or why not. That review is what provides insights for improved decision making in the future, so a version that stops once the action is taken omits the component the framework depends on for learning.

drills.los_text: explain how the practices, policies, or conduct does or does not violate the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct
drills.reading_name: Application of the Code and Standards: Level III

questions.stem: Adebayo, who selects investments for a national development institution, quickly sets the order in which three competing projects will be funded; each project is backed by a different senior government official. Compliance with Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis most likely required her to:

options.A: defer the sequencing decision to a higher authority.
options.B: disclose the political influences on her decision.
options.C: weigh each project on its own investment merit.

rationales.A: Deferring the sequencing decision to a higher governmental authority would not mitigate, and may in fact enhance, political influence on the investment decision, rather than ensure that each project is objectively considered for its individual investment merit. Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis requires Adebayo herself to exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness and to have a reasonable and adequate basis for the decision, and she cannot discharge that duty by handing the decision up the chain.
rationales.B: Disclosing outside negative situational influences or conflicts of interest does not replace the need to act with independent and objective judgment when analyzing and selecting investment opportunities. Disclosure may be required under other standards, but under Standard V(A) it is no substitute for an independent, adequately supported basis for the sequencing decision, so disclosure alone would not have satisfied the standard.
rationales.C: Adebayo faced political pressures from senior governmental supporters of each project, and her quick decision was made on political, not investment or financial, considerations. Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis requires members to exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness and to have a reasonable and adequate basis to support investment action, so she had to thoroughly and independently investigate each potential investment and be resolute in maintaining her independence and objectivity in order to act in the best interests of the institution and its investors. Deferring the decision to a higher governmental authority would not mitigate and may in fact enhance political influence, and disclosing the situational influences would not replace the duty of independent, objective judgment.

questions.stem: Adebayo invests on behalf of a national development institution whose investors are informed up front that investment return is not the single determining factor in its investment decisions. In a meeting with a prospective hedge fund investor, she assures the fund that the institution will prioritize maximizing return. Her assurance is most likely:

options.A: improper, because it misrepresents the institution's mandate.
options.B: improper, because hedge funds may not invest in the institution.
options.C: proper, because sophisticated investors treat it as aspirational.

rationales.A: The institution operates under a dual mandate: it invests in projects that have both a beneficial socioeconomic impact and a positive expected investment return. That mandate is in contrast to traditional investment mandates that focus only on return on investment regardless of outside or other impact, and the institution's investors are informed up front that investment return is not the single determining factor for its investment decisions. Any assurance by Adebayo to the hedge fund or to other investors that promises a set rate of return or prioritizes return maximization is contrary to that mandate and misstates the basis on which the money is actually managed, and is therefore a violation of Standard III(C) Suitability.
rationales.B: No standard or rule bars hedge funds from investing in a development institution, and the investor's identity is not the defect. What makes the assurance improper is its content: promising returns on a basis inconsistent with the institution's dual socioeconomic-impact and investment-return mandate.
rationales.C: Investor sophistication is no defense. The institution's investors are informed up front that investment return is not the single determining factor for its investment decisions, so an assurance that promises a set rate of return or prioritizes return maximization misstates the mandate the money is actually managed against, however experienced the investor. The assurance is contrary to the dual mandate and violates Standard III(C) Suitability.

questions.stem: Corrales, who works for a hedge fund, reads the fund's research on a development institution and learns that the fund intends to invest in it. He buys shares of the institution for his own account before the fund begins buying, and the shares rise once the fund has completed its purchases. His personal purchase is most likely:

options.A: improper, because he relied on the fund's research.
options.B: proper, because the fund was not disadvantaged.
options.C: improper, because the fund's buying lifted his shares.

rationales.A: Use of the hedge fund's research is not the defect. Purchasing the same investments as your employer, or investing in the same assets as your clients, does not necessarily create a conflict of interest, although best practice recommends that such co-investing be disclosed. What makes this trade a violation is its sequence: Corrales bought before the fund did and so captured for himself the appreciation the fund's own transaction produced.
rationales.B: The practice is unethical and violates Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions even if his personal investment does not disadvantage the hedge fund in any way. Transactions for clients and employers have priority over personal transactions; buying ahead of the fund's investment let Corrales capture for himself the price appreciation the fund's transaction produced, and he should have waited until after the fund had completed its investment.
rationales.C: After the hedge fund invests, the value of the shares increases, benefiting Corrales through an increase in the value of the personal investment he made beforehand. The practice is unethical and violates Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions even if his personal investment does not disadvantage the hedge fund in any way, and Corrales should have waited to invest until after the fund had completed its investment. Purchasing the same investments as your employer, or investing in the same assets as your clients, does not necessarily create a conflict of interest, although best practice recommends that such co-investing be disclosed.

questions.stem: Corrales pays undocumented 'deal fees' to locally connected intermediaries who use their official contacts to introduce investment opportunities to his firm, and he records the payments as operating expenses. The payments are most likely:

options.A: permitted, because local law tolerates facilitation fees.
options.B: acceptable, because operating expenses is a broad category.
options.C: improper, because they are bribes, not subadvisory fees.

rationales.A: Local tolerance of facilitation payments does not sanitize the conduct. The deal fees are corrupt transactions paid for official connections, they are not supported by any documentation that details legitimate investment expenses, and Corrales's conduct would most likely violate applicable anti-bribery laws, so Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law is violated rather than satisfied.
rationales.B: Operating expenses is not a category broad enough to absorb corrupt payments. Recording the deal fees that way misrepresents what they are, and no documentation details them as legitimate investment expenses, so the accounting treatment compounds the underlying misconduct instead of excusing it.
rationales.C: Although it is acceptable to hire subadvisers to assist in sourcing investment opportunities, Corrales is not hiring a subadviser to assist in the investment decision-making process; he is essentially engaged in bribery and in facilitating local corruption. The deal fees are corrupt transactions and are not supported by any documentation that details legitimate investment expenses, and his conduct would most likely violate applicable anti-bribery laws, so Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law is the standard implicated. An adviser who does hire subadvisers must ensure they have the necessary knowledge or expertise to meet the need for diligence and thoroughness, but the defect here is not the delegation; it is the corrupt payment and its misreporting as a legitimate operating expense.

questions.stem: The right to use the CFA designation after the charter has been awarded is most likely:

options.A: dependent on annual dues and a conduct statement.
options.B: permanent, in the same way a university degree is.
options.C: secure once all three exams have been passed.

rationales.A: The CFA designation is not like a degree from a university. Once granted the right to use the designation, individuals must also satisfy CFA Institute membership requirements, which include paying dues and submitting a Professional Conduct Statement annually, in order to maintain the right to refer to themselves as CFA charterholders. A charterholder who stops paying dues has a lapsed membership, and until membership is reactivated she must not use the CFA designation or present herself as a charterholder, although she may state that she was previously a CFA Institute member.
rationales.B: Treating the charter as a permanent, unconditional credential is the misconception at issue. Unlike a university degree, the designation requires annual maintenance: continued membership, payment of dues, and submission of a Professional Conduct Statement each year. A lapse in any of those suspends the right to use the marks.
rationales.C: Passing the examinations earns the charter but does not maintain the right to use the designation, which depends on current CFA Institute membership rather than on the examinations. Where dues have not been paid, membership is considered lapsed, and until membership is reactivated the individual must not use the CFA designation or present herself as a charterholder to clients or potential investors; she may, however, state that she was previously a CFA Institute member.

questions.stem: In a meeting with a potential investor, Mehrotra hears his colleague Adebayo refer to herself as a CFA charterholder, knowing that her CFA Institute membership has lapsed for nonpayment of dues, and he says nothing. His silence most likely:

options.A: lies outside a Code that governs only his own conduct.
options.B: assists Adebayo's violation, because he knew of the lapse.
options.C: breaches nothing, since he made no false statement to the investor.

rationales.A: Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law is not limited to a member's own misconduct. It prohibits members from knowingly participating or assisting in the violations of others and requires members to dissociate from any unethical or illegal conduct, a colleague's included, so Mehrotra cannot treat Adebayo's misrepresentation as none of his concern.
rationales.B: Mehrotra hears Adebayo refer to herself as a charterholder, but he knows that because she has not paid her dues, her CFA Institute membership has lapsed. Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law prohibits members from knowingly participating or assisting in the violations of others, and by keeping silent about false information given to a potential investor when doing so is potentially harmful, his behavior constitutes assisting in the violation even though there is no active conduct on his part. Best practice, although difficult, would be for Mehrotra to address Adebayo directly and ask her to reinstate her membership or correct the statement made to the potential investor; if she refuses to take corrective action, he could bring the conduct to the attention of the firm's compliance department, and he should dissociate from the activity by not participating in any future sales meetings with her.
rationales.C: Making no false statement himself is not enough. Standard I(A) prohibits knowingly participating or assisting in the violations of others, so silence that lets a colleague's misrepresentation stand before a potential investor is within its reach even absent any active conduct, and the standard also requires dissociation from the conduct.

questions.stem: Regarding a candidate's discussion of an exam she has sat, Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs most likely:

options.A: requires candidates to keep their exam experience confidential.
options.B: permits naming the topic areas tested if question wording is withheld.
options.C: permits discussion of the exam experience only in general terms.

rationales.A: This overstates the duty. Candidates can discuss their exam experience in general terms, including how hard they found a given topic; a candidate saying the ethics topic in the exam was difficult is not in violation of Standard VII(A). What candidates may not do is provide specific information about exam questions or about the curriculum subjects that are or are not tested.
rationales.B: Standard VII(A) reaches more than the wording of questions. Candidates cannot provide specific information about the exam questions or about the curriculum subjects that are or are not tested on the exam. Although ethics is known to be one of 10 topic areas tested, there may be no exam question on material nonpublic information, so a candidate saying there were no exam questions on insider information violates the standard even with no question wording revealed.
rationales.C: Candidates can discuss their exam experience in general terms, but they cannot provide specific information about the exam questions or about the curriculum subjects that are or are not tested on the exam. A candidate saying the ethics topic in the exam was difficult is not in violation of Standard VII(A), whereas a candidate saying there were no exam questions on insider information would violate it, because that reveals coverage. Soliciting information about specific exam questions from candidates in order to improve future preparatory classes likewise violates Standard VII(A).

questions.stem: Hockett's research team acted on a pending change to one of BankGlobal's in-house recommendations in discretionary client accounts before notifying the firm's other clients. BankGlobal's clients pay the bank for its research, and an investor who wants access to it can obtain it by becoming a client. Regarding the application of Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information to the team's conduct, the most accurate statement is that:

options.A: the pending recommendation change was material nonpublic information.
options.B: the general investing public relies on the firm's recommendations.
options.C: the recommendations are produced for all of the bank's client accounts.

rationales.A: The firm's own pending change to an in-house recommendation is not material nonpublic information about an issuer. Information is material if it would significantly alter the total mix of information currently available about a security, and for BankGlobal's own research to clear that bar there would have to be a clear indication that the general investing public relies on it. The failure here is preferential treatment of some client accounts over others, which is governed by Standard III(B) Fair Dealing rather than Standard II(A).
rationales.B: There is no indication that BankGlobal's recommendations are distributed to, or highly valued by, the general investing public. Clients pay BankGlobal for its research, and an investor who wants access to it can obtain it by becoming a client of the bank, so the research does not meet the materiality test Standard II(A) requires. The violation is instead one of fair dealing under Standard III(B).
rationales.C: The research team develops its recommendations for the management of all of BankGlobal's client accounts, and those clients pay BankGlobal for its research; investors who would like access to that research can obtain it by becoming clients of the bank. Information is material if it would significantly alter the total mix of information currently available about a security, and to be considered material there would need to be a clear indication that the general investing public relies on BankGlobal's information. Nothing indicates that BankGlobal's recommendations are distributed to or highly valued by the general investing public, so the team did not hold material nonpublic information. Acting on the pending recommendation change in discretionary accounts ahead of other clients is therefore a Standard III(B) Fair Dealing issue, not a Standard II(A) issue.

questions.stem: Lopez presents a model portfolio's performance to the Kochanskis, prospective clients whose level of investment knowledge is unknown to Lopez, using the average of the returns of the four funds that make up the portfolio. Under Standard III(D) Performance Presentation, the presentation is most likely:

options.A: acceptable, as the form of the presentation fits the audience.
options.B: acceptable where an appendix also shows each fund's own return.
options.C: prohibited, as each fund's return must be shown separately.

rationales.A: Using an average of the four funds' performance to present the model portfolio's performance is acceptable, because the Kochanskis' knowledge of investments is unknown to Lopez, and this easy-to-understand approach is appropriate for sharing information with novice investors. The guidance for Standard III(D) provides that members and candidates can also meet their obligations under the standard by considering the knowledge and sophistication of the audience to whom a performance presentation is addressed. The presentation obligation is satisfied by matching the form of the presentation to that audience, not by maximizing detail.
rationales.B: No appendix requirement exists under Standard III(D). The obligation can be met by considering the knowledge and sophistication of the audience to whom the performance presentation is addressed, and an easy-to-understand average of the four funds is an appropriate presentation for novice investors such as the Kochanskis, whose level of investment knowledge is unknown to Lopez. Adding each fund's individual return in an appendix may be informative, but it is not a condition of compliance.
rationales.C: Separate presentation of each fund's return is not mandated in all cases. Standard III(D) requires fair, accurate and complete presentation, and it is met in part by considering the knowledge and sophistication of the audience addressed. For prospective clients whose investment knowledge is unknown to Lopez, an average of the four funds is an acceptable, easy-to-understand simplification rather than a prohibited one.
