questions.stem: Hockett invests 15%-20% of his clients' portfolios in high-beta stocks and tells them the position is low risk, while their long-term conservative objectives and investment policy statements are left unchanged. Under Standard III(C) Suitability, the most accurate statement about the allocation and Hockett's description of it is that:

options.A: his description of the position as low risk is incorrect.
options.B: the allocation diversifies and so lowers overall portfolio risk.
options.C: the unchanged policy statements make the allocation suitable.

rationales.A: High-beta stocks are not low risk, so Hockett's description of the position is incorrect. Standard III(C) provides that when a member is responsible for managing a portfolio to a specific mandate, strategy or style, the member must make only investment recommendations or take only investment actions consistent with the stated objectives and constraints of that portfolio. Investing 15%-20% of accounts that carry long-term conservative objectives in high-beta stocks is contrary to the long-term risk profile established in those investment policy statements, so Standard III(C) is violated. That the clients' investment objectives and investment policy statements are unchanged is irrelevant: Hockett changed the investment strategy of his clients in an attempt to reap the short-term rewards offered by his firm's new compensation arrangement, not in response to any change in clients' investment needs.
rationales.B: High-beta stocks carry above-market risk by their nature, and a 15%-20% allocation to them runs contrary to the long-term conservative risk profile established in the clients' investment policy statements. Diversification does not reconcile the position with the mandate Hockett is responsible for managing to, so the actions remain inconsistent with the stated objectives and constraints that Standard III(C) requires him to respect.
rationales.C: That the clients' investment objectives and investment policy statements are unchanged is irrelevant. Hockett is responsible for managing to the mandate those documents establish, and taking investment actions contrary to the long-term conservative risk profile they set violates Standard III(C) whether or not the documents themselves were revised. The change of strategy was made to capture short-term rewards under the firm's new compensation arrangement rather than in response to any change in client needs.

questions.stem: Lopez posts on a personal social media account, seen mainly by former high school classmates, that the Kochanskis have become clients of the firm. Under Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, the post is most likely:

options.A: permissible, as the post reached only a private audience.
options.B: a violation, as the post implied the clients' financial standing.
options.C: a violation, as the post revealed the client relationship.

rationales.A: The breadth of the audience is not the test. Standard III(E) extends beyond the investment industry to the population as a whole, so disclosing client information to any unauthorized party breaches it, whether the recipients are the general public or a private group of former classmates. Posting to high school friends is not exempt.
rationales.B: Naming the Kochanskis as new clients is itself the violation. Standard III(E) requires that all information about current, former or prospective clients be kept confidential, not just information about their investments or dollar amounts, and that includes the existence of the client relationship. Nothing about the clients' financial standing had to be revealed for the breach to occur.
rationales.C: Standard III(E) requires that all information about current, former or prospective clients be kept confidential, not just information about their investments or dollar amounts. Posting the name of the Kochanskis as new clients therefore violated the required confidentiality, because the existence of the relationship is itself client information. That confidentiality extends beyond the investment industry to the population as a whole, so a post directed at a personal audience of former high school classmates is not exempt.

questions.stem: Plume, a sell-side analyst at Global, covers companies controlled by CB, and the relationships among Plume, CB, its subsidiaries and Global are disclosed in the offering prospectus but not in his research. Under Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts, the prospectus disclosure is most likely:

options.A: necessary but not sufficient, as it may not be prominent.
options.B: insufficient, as investors rarely read offering documents.
options.C: sufficient, as the prospectus is the governing legal document.

rationales.A: That the relationships between Plume, CB, its subsidiaries and Global are disclosed in the offering prospectus is necessary but not sufficient to meet Standard VI(A), because the prospectus may not communicate the information effectively or in a prominent manner. Standard VI(A) requires that disclosures be prominent, be delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information effectively, which means the conflict must also be disclosed where it operates, in the research Plume produces.
rationales.B: The test under Standard VI(A) is not investor reading habits. Prospectus disclosure is necessary but not sufficient because it may not communicate the conflict effectively or in a prominent manner; the standard requires prominent, plain-language disclosure that communicates the relevant information effectively, delivered with the research in which the conflict operates.
rationales.C: Satisfying a legal disclosure requirement elsewhere is necessary but not sufficient under Standard VI(A). Disclosure must be prominent, in plain language, and effective in communicating the conflict, and a prospectus may do none of those things for a reader of Plume's research. The research itself must carry the disclosure rather than relying on the governing offering document.

questions.stem: Plume owns CB preferred shares and CB common stock options, and CB holds voting control of both STRX and APBX, two companies he covers. Under Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts, the most accurate statement about Plume's interest in STRX and APBX is that:

options.A: he has no beneficial ownership interest in the two companies.
options.B: his parent-company holdings confer an interest in CB alone.
options.C: he has a beneficial interest even without direct share ownership.

rationales.A: Beneficial ownership includes an indirect pecuniary interest, so direct holdings are not required. Plume's ownership of CB's preferred shares and common stock options, together with CB's voting control of STRX and APBX, gives him a beneficial ownership interest in each of those companies, and that interest creates a conflict of interest requiring disclosure.
rationales.B: CB's voting control of STRX and APBX carries Plume's parent-company holdings through to the subsidiaries. Under Standard VI(A), members beneficially own securities when they have a direct or indirect pecuniary interest in them, have the power to direct their voting, or have the power to dispose of them, so the interest created by preferred shares and stock options in a controlling parent is not confined to that parent.
rationales.C: Plume does not need to own shares in STRX and APBX directly to have a beneficial interest in the two companies. His ownership of CB's preferred shares and its common stock options, along with CB's voting control of each company, gives him a beneficial ownership interest in STRX and APBX. Under Standard VI(A), members beneficially own securities if they have a direct or indirect pecuniary interest in them, have the power to direct the voting, or have the power to dispose of them. The situation creates a conflict of interest that requires disclosure.

questions.stem: Plume, a sell-side analyst at Global, covers companies controlled by CB, a holding company whose subsidiaries Global takes public. Plume's compensation at Global includes a bonus tied to the gross proceeds of initial public offerings that Global underwrites and on whose deal teams he serves. Under Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity, the arrangement most likely:

options.A: violates the standard once a report he writes proves biased.
options.B: violates the standard by encouraging biased research coverage.
options.C: complies with the standard, as it rewards the entire team.

rationales.A: The arrangement compromises independence prospectively, so no skewed report has to appear before the standard is engaged. Linking analyst remuneration to banking assignments creates exactly the incentive the guidance for Standard I(B) tells firms to remove, and the conflict must be managed, disclosed or eliminated regardless of what any individual report later says.
rationales.B: As a sell-side analyst, Plume may be encouraged by Global or CB to write potentially biased research reports about particular companies, namely those in CB's portfolio, to the exclusion of covering companies that may be more suitable for Global's clients. The guidance for Standard I(B) states that compensation arrangements should not link analyst remuneration directly to investment banking assignments in which the analysts may participate as a team member, and that having analysts work with investment bankers is appropriate only when the conflicts are adequately and effectively managed and disclosed. Firm managers have a responsibility to provide an environment in which analysts are neither coerced nor enticed into issuing research that does not reflect their true opinions, and firms should require public disclosure of actual conflicts of interest to investors. Global can avoid the conflict by removing this incentive from Plume's compensation package.
rationales.C: A team-wide payout does not cure the conflict. The guidance for Standard I(B) states that compensation arrangements should not link analyst remuneration directly to investment banking assignments in which the analysts may participate as a team member, and a bonus tied to deal proceeds still gives Plume a personal financial stake in favorable coverage of the companies in CB's portfolio, whatever the rating he nominally assigns.

questions.stem: After resigning from Kodiak, Benning used her personal social media accounts, and no records of the firm, to contact clients she had served there. Under Standard IV(A) Loyalty, her contact with those clients most likely:

options.A: violates the standard's bar on soliciting former clients.
options.B: complies with the standard, which permits post-employment contact.
options.C: violates the standard, as the relationships are Kodiak's property.

rationales.A: Standard IV(A) imposes no such continuing bar on approaching a former employer's clients. The guidance provides that once employment has ended, the standard does not prohibit a former employee from contacting clients of the prior firm, as long as the contact information does not come from the records of the former employer and the outreach does not violate an applicable agreement, such as a non-solicitation covenant. Benning's duty of loyalty ended with her employment.
rationales.B: Benning did not solicit clients until after she resigned from Kodiak. She used her personal social media platforms to connect with those clients, she did not contact them until after her resignation, and she did not use material from Kodiak without the firm's permission. Under the guidance for Standard IV(A), once employment has ended the standard does not prohibit contacting clients of the former employer, provided the contact information does not come from the records of the former employer and the outreach does not violate an applicable agreement.
rationales.C: Client relationships are not firm property in a way that survives the member's departure. What Standard IV(A) protects is the employer's property, including records, files and client lists, so contact made after resignation, through the member's own social media accounts and without using any material from the firm, misappropriates nothing.

questions.stem: Benning received a signing bonus from Global when she joined the firm, and clients she had served at Kodiak subsequently moved their accounts to Global. For Benning, the signing bonus is most likely:

options.A: additional compensation under Standard IV(B).
options.B: a referral fee for the moved accounts under Standard VI(C).
options.C: a conflict of interest to disclose under Standard VI(A).

rationales.A: Standard IV(B) describes additional compensation as gifts, benefits, compensation or consideration that competes with, or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with, the employer's interest absent written consent from all parties involved. Such arrangements generally concern conflicts the member has with the employer, not with clients and prospects. Global, the employer, paid the bonus itself for services provided, so it is not additional compensation in that sense; the conflict that must be addressed runs to Benning's clients under Standard VI(A).
rationales.B: Standard VI(C) defines referral fees as any compensation, consideration or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services. The signing bonus was paid by Global to Benning as an employee for services provided, not for recommending a product or service to anyone, so it is not a referral fee, whatever the accounts that later moved.
rationales.C: Referral fees are compensation received for the recommendation of products or services, and the signing bonus is not one: Global paid it to Benning as an employee rather than for a recommendation. Additional compensation under Standard IV(B) means gifts, benefits, compensation or consideration that competes with, or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with, the employer's interest absent written consent from all parties, and such arrangements generally refer to conflicts with the employer rather than with clients and prospects, so the bonus is not additional compensation in that sense either. The bonus could, however, reasonably be expected to impair Benning's independence and objectivity or to interfere with her respective duties to her clients, so Standard VI(A) requires her to avoid it or to disclose it fully to her Kodiak clients as an actual or potential conflict of interest.

questions.stem: Benning and Global allocate shares in the FTSX initial public offering only to institutional clients that agree to buy additional shares once FTSX begins trading. Considering Standard II(B) Market Manipulation and Standard III(B) Fair Dealing, the allocation practice most likely:

options.A: violates both standards.
options.B: violates only Standard III(B).
options.C: violates neither standard.

rationales.A: The guidance for Standard II(B) Market Manipulation states that transaction-based manipulation involves instances where a member or candidate knows or should know that his or her actions could distort the price of a security. Benning and Global are artificially creating demand for FTSX shares, and raising the price on the first day of trading, by allocating IPO shares only to clients who plan to purchase additional shares on that first day. The practice also violates Standard III(B) Fair Dealing, because Benning is not treating all of her institutional clients fairly when she allocates IPO shares only to those clients who agree to purchase additional shares after FTSX begins trading; the overall criteria and policy Global uses to determine client allocations violate Standard III(B) as well.
rationales.B: Two provisions are genuinely implicated, not one. Allocating shares only to the clients who agree to buy more does deny the remaining institutional clients the fair treatment Standard III(B) requires, but conditioning allocations on aftermarket purchases is also transaction-based manipulation of the first-day price under Standard II(B), since Benning knows or should know the arrangement could distort that price.
rationales.C: Conditioning an allocation on aftermarket buying is a manipulation device rather than legitimate marketing of an oversubscribed offering. It artificially creates demand and raises the first-day price, which is transaction-based manipulation under Standard II(B), and it denies fair treatment to the institutional clients who do not agree to the tie-in, which breaches Standard III(B).

questions.stem: Benning made and initialed changes to her client Deacon's option account forms and signed his Account Linking form, having obtained his approval by telephone only. Under the Standards, that telephone approval is most likely:

options.A: adequate, Benning having acted in Deacon's best interest.
options.B: short of the written authorization the form requires.
options.C: effective as Deacon's consent to sign on his behalf.

rationales.A: Acting in the client's best interest does not substitute for the client's own authorization. Even if Benning believed that the changes she made and initialed on the Option Account Application and Agreement form, and the Account Linking form she signed, served Deacon's interests, those changes cannot be implemented without Deacon's own written approval. Her belief about his interests therefore does not relieve her of the need for his personal signature.
rationales.B: The approval Benning received over the telephone to sign the Account Linking form is insufficient. Benning needs Deacon to personally sign the authorization. Even if Benning was acting in Deacon's best interests by making and initialing the changes on the Option Account Application and Agreement form and by signing the Account Linking form, these changes cannot be implemented without Deacon's own written approval, and they are therefore in violation of the Standards.
rationales.C: Telephone authorization is not valid consent for this purpose. The change cannot be effected without Deacon's own written, personally signed authorization, so signing the form on his behalf was not permissible. A verbal approval relayed by telephone leaves no client-executed record of the authorization the form requires.

questions.stem: In marketing materials, Hill calls the VCF the best-performing fund and reports its returns, disclosing that the figures are gross of fees, or "pre-fees." Hill's statements are most likely:

options.A: not a violation of the Standards.
options.B: a violation of Standard III(D), net-of-fees figures being required.
options.C: a violation of Standard I(C), the best-performing claim overstating fact.

rationales.A: There is no evidence to suggest Hill's statements are false or opinion based. In speaking about the fund's performance, Hill is stating facts, and Hill states that the performance is gross of fees, or "pre-fees." Standard III(D) Performance Presentation requires that when communicating investment performance information, members and candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that it is fair, accurate, and complete. The guidance for Standard III(D) states that members and candidates can meet their obligations by including disclosures that fully explain the performance results being reported — for example, stating when appropriate that results are simulated when model results are used, clearly indicating when the performance record is that of a prior entity, or disclosing whether the performance is gross of fees, net of fees, or after tax. Hill's statement that the returns are gross of fees is exactly such a disclosure.
rationales.B: Standard III(D) imposes no net-of-fees requirement and does not forbid gross-of-fees figures. It requires that performance information be fair, accurate, and complete, and its guidance expressly contemplates disclosing whether performance is gross of fees, net of fees, or after tax. Hill stated that the returns were gross of fees, or "pre-fees," which satisfies that disclosure requirement, so presenting the returns on a gross basis is not itself a violation.
rationales.C: There is no evidence that Hill's statements are false or opinion based. Describing the VCF by its performance record is a statement of fact about that record, not a guarantee of future results or an opinion dressed as fact, and Hill discloses the basis on which the returns are reported. Standard I(C) Misrepresentation reaches knowing misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities, and Hill has made none.

questions.stem: Hill appears on television talk shows and accepts gift bags from the shows' sponsors, none of which are clients of his employer, LL, or of the VCF. The gift bags most likely fall outside Standard IV(B) because they:

options.A: fall below a fixed monetary threshold.
options.B: do not conflict with his employer's interest.
options.C: are received in connection with public appearances.

rationales.A: No monetary threshold defines Standard IV(B). The operative test is whether the gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration competes with, or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with, the employer's interest absent written consent from all parties involved. Value may bear on that judgment, but it is not itself the standard, and a gift of modest value that did conflict with the employer's interest would still have to be refused or consented to.
rationales.B: Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements provides that members and candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved. Hill's appearances on these shows do not create a conflict of interest with the interests of LL or the VCF. The sponsors are not clients of LL, and their gift bags neither compete with nor create a conflict with his employer's interests.
rationales.C: No categorical exemption exists for gifts received in connection with public appearances. The operative test under Standard IV(B) is whether the benefit competes with, or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with, the employer's interest. These sponsor gift bags fall outside the standard because they do not conflict with the interests of LL or the VCF, not because of the setting in which Hill received them.

questions.stem: Portman sells his shares in a listed company after the Sky News Business Channel reports that the company's chief investment officer and several of its board members have sold theirs, having also heard unconfirmed internal rumors that a senior executive may resign. Portman's sale is most likely:

options.A: permissible, the officer and board sales being publicly reported.
options.B: permissible only after a thirty-day waiting period.
options.C: impermissible, given the unconfirmed resignation rumors.

rationales.A: Portman's decision to sell is not based on material nonpublic information, because this information was publicly reported: he learned of the chief investment officer's and the board members' sales from the Sky News Business Channel. Publicly available news does not constitute material nonpublic information, so he is not in violation of Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information.
rationales.B: The Code and Standards impose no waiting period once information is genuinely public. Standard II(A) turns on whether the information relied on is both material and nonpublic, not on how recently it was disseminated, and the officer and board member sales Portman acted on had already been reported publicly.
rationales.C: Portman does not know definitively whether the executive is resigning, and his decision to sell was based on the publicly reported officer and board member sales. Possessing an unconfirmed rumor alongside public information does not convert a trade made on public news into a violation of Standard II(A).

questions.stem: On learning of a complaint that her subordinate Graeme may have violated the Code and Standards, Balmer called Graeme into her office, sat in on his meeting with the client Milgram, and reviewed the account and the IPS. Balmer most likely complied with Standard IV(C) because she:

options.A: obtained Graeme's assurances that the conduct would not recur.
options.B: promptly initiated her own assessment of the conduct.
options.C: established that the complaint was unfounded.

rationales.A: Relying on an employee's statements about the extent of a violation, or on assurances that the wrongdoing will not reoccur, is not enough under Standard IV(C). Balmer complied because she promptly initiated an assessment herself — calling Graeme into her office, sitting in on the meeting with Milgram, and reviewing the account and the IPS — not because of anything Graeme told her.
rationales.B: Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires that members and candidates make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards. Under the guidance for this standard, once a supervisor learns that an employee has violated, or may have violated, the law or the Code and Standards, the supervisor must promptly initiate an assessment to determine the extent of the wrongdoing; relying on the employee's statements about the extent of the violation, or on assurances that it will not reoccur, is not enough. Balmer's active investigation — calling Graeme in, attending the Milgram meeting, and reviewing the account and the IPS — meets the requirements of Standard IV(C).
rationales.C: Compliance with Standard IV(C) is judged by the supervisor's response, that is, whether she promptly initiated an assessment to determine the extent of the possible wrongdoing, and not by whether the complaint ultimately proves to have merit. Balmer's prompt investigation would satisfy the standard whatever the complaint's outcome.

questions.stem: Tan and Chuong share in the fees their own firm, GHB, earns from MGM2, a client the two of them brought on themselves. That fee-sharing arrangement is best described as:

options.A: a referral fee.
options.B: a reward for business development.
options.C: an undisclosed conflict of interest.

rationales.A: A referral fee is compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services. Tan and Chuong did not refer MGM2 to GHB; they brought MGM2 on as a client of GHB, their own firm. Being compensated for that business development effort therefore does not make the payment a referral fee.
rationales.B: The fee-sharing arrangement is a reward paid to Tan and Chuong for their efforts to bring MGM2 on as a client. The fee arrangement is not a referral fee, because Tan and Chuong did not refer MGM2 to GHB, and a referral fee is compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services.
rationales.C: The case facts provide no evidence that a conflict of interest is present. The fee-sharing is a legitimate reward for bringing in a client of the firm, so it triggers no disclosure obligation under Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts.

questions.stem: Hie, a person connected to GHB's client MGM2, hires Chuong's son into an executive position at Hie's own firm, and Chuong says nothing about it. With respect to the Standards, Chuong's failure to disclose her son's employment is most likely:

options.A: a violation of Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts.
options.B: not a violation of the Standards.
options.C: a violation of Standard I(C) Misrepresentation.

rationales.A: Hie's hiring of Chuong's son in an executive position at Hie's firm could reasonably be expected to impair Chuong's independence and objectivity with respect to interactions between MGM2 and GHB. A personal relationship, here through her son's employment, with a person connected to a client of the firm creates a potential conflict of interest, and Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts requires Chuong to disclose that conflict.
rationales.B: Standard VI(A) reaches any matter that could reasonably be expected to impair independence and objectivity, not only matters that pay the member directly. An executive position for her son at a firm connected to a client could compromise Chuong's objectivity with respect to interactions between MGM2 and GHB even though the benefit runs to her son rather than to her, so disclosure is required.
rationales.C: The failure here is the nondisclosure of a conflict of interest, which is the domain of Standard VI(A), rather than an affirmative false statement. This situation is not a violation of Standard I(C) Misrepresentation, because by not disclosing information about her son, Chuong did not knowingly make any misrepresentation relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities.

questions.stem: Sim's client Hie asks her to destroy the notes she took during their meetings, which support the recommendations she made and the actions she took for him. Sim's duty with respect to those notes is most likely to:

options.A: destroy them under Standard III(E).
options.B: treat them as personal working papers.
options.C: retain them under Standard V(C).

rationales.A: Retaining the notes in no way compromises Sim's duty of confidentiality to Hie under Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, and that standard does not require destroying documentation that supports an adviser's recommendations and actions. The destruction of the documentation is also not directly related to the actions considered necessary under Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care.
rationales.B: Notes taken from client meetings are supporting documentation, not private working papers beyond the reach of the Standards. Standard V(C) Record Retention requires members and candidates to develop and maintain appropriate records to support their investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and other client communications, which is precisely what these notes do.
rationales.C: Sim has a duty to her firm to retain records supporting her recommendations to, and her actions for, clients of the firm. Keeping these records in no way compromises her duty of confidentiality to Hie under Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, and the destruction of the documentation is not directly related to the actions considered necessary under Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care. Standard V(C) Record Retention requires members and candidates to develop and maintain appropriate records to support their investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and other client communications.

questions.stem: Sim told her supervisor, Yousoff, that she suspects a client of laundering money, and Yousoff took no action toward resolving her concerns. Sim's most appropriate next step is to:

options.A: seek the advice of the firm's compliance department.
options.B: take no further action.
options.C: report the matter to her jurisdiction's regulator.

rationales.A: Informing Yousoff produced no action toward resolving Sim's concerns. The guidance for Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law recommends that when in doubt about the appropriate action to undertake, a member or candidate seek the advice of compliance personnel or legal counsel concerning legal requirements, and that if a potential violation is being committed by a fellow employee, it may also be prudent for the member or candidate to seek the advice of the firm's compliance department or legal counsel. Escalation within the firm therefore precedes any external reporting.
rationales.B: Informing Yousoff produced no action toward resolving Sim's concerns, so her obligations are not discharged by that step alone. Under the guidance for Standard I(A), she must escalate the matter by seeking the advice of compliance personnel or legal counsel.
rationales.C: The Code and Standards do not compel members and candidates to report violations to their governmental or regulatory organizations unless such disclosure is mandatory under applicable law, although such disclosure may be prudent under certain circumstances. With Yousoff having taken no action, the recommended next step is to seek the advice of the firm's compliance department or legal counsel.

questions.stem: At the inception of the advisory relationship, Sim's new client gives her a fact sheet stating his desired strategy of holding only short-term government securities, and no investment policy statement (IPS) is prepared. Under Standard III(C) Suitability, Sim's reliance on the fact sheet is most likely:

options.A: deficient, absent a fully formed IPS.
options.B: adequate as a statement of the client's strategy.
options.C: excusable, given the risk-free securities.

rationales.A: A client's statement regarding his or her desired investment strategy, especially without a fully formed IPS, does not meet the requirements of Standard III(C) Suitability. The fact sheet does not provide enough information for Sim to develop an appropriate IPS. The standard requires that when an advisory relationship exists, members and candidates must gather client information at the inception of the relationship, including the client's financial circumstances, personal data such as age and occupation that are relevant to investment decisions, attitudes toward risk, and objectives in investing, and this information should be incorporated into a written IPS.
rationales.B: A bare client declaration of a desired strategy, without the required inquiry and a formed IPS, does not meet the inception requirements of Standard III(C). The standard requires the adviser to gather the client's financial circumstances, relevant personal data, attitudes toward risk, and investment objectives at the inception of the relationship and to incorporate them into a written IPS; the client's own statement of strategy is an input to that inquiry rather than a substitute for it.
rationales.C: The safety of the initial product does not excuse the inquiry. Standard III(C) requires gathering client information at the inception of the relationship, including financial circumstances, personal data such as age and occupation, attitudes toward risk, and objectives in investing, incorporated into a written IPS, regardless of how safe the first investment appears.

questions.stem: Sim wishes to discuss Hie's account with board members Tan and Chuong. Under Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, she may do so most likely:

options.A: only when disclosure is required by law or concerns illegal activities.
options.B: in any case where the client has granted permission.
options.C: under no circumstances.

rationales.A: This omits the client-permission exception. Disclosure required by law and the disclosure of illegal activities are not the only circumstances in which confidence may be broken. Hie authorized the disclosure by telling Sim to seek information as needed from board members Tan and Chuong, so Sim may speak with them without violating the Code and Standards.
rationales.B: Under Standard III(E), a member or candidate can break confidence when permission is granted by the client. Hie has given his permission to Sim by telling her to seek information as needed from board members Tan and Chuong, so Sim is not in violation of the Code and Standards. III(E) is applicable when (1) the member receives information because of his or her special ability to conduct a portion of the client's business and (2) the member receives information that arises from or is relevant to that portion of the client's business.
rationales.C: Standard III(E) is not absolute: it permits breaking confidence when the client grants permission, which Hie did by directing Sim to consult the board members as needed.

questions.stem: Madam Tan is retired, holds fixed deposits and lower-risk energy utility stocks, wishes to invest more of her portfolio in conservative equities, and says she is unsure what oil futures are or how they work. She asks Sim to buy her an oil-linked structured note. Under Standard III(C) Suitability, the note is most likely:

options.A: unsuitable, because retail investors are prohibited from holding structured products.
options.B: suitable, because the request came from the client.
options.C: unsuitable, given her investment objectives.

rationales.A: No prohibition bars retail investors from structured products. What makes the note unsuitable is the mismatch with Madam Tan's conservative profile of fixed deposits and lower-risk energy utility stocks, not a product-level ban.
rationales.B: Responsibility does not shift to the client because the client initiated the request. Standard III(C) requires members and candidates to make reasonable efforts to balance clients' trading requests with their responsibility to follow the agreed-on investment policy statement, and the note conflicts with Madam Tan's conservative, fixed-deposit-and-utilities profile; accurate execution is not a defense.
rationales.C: Sim violated Standard III(C) Suitability, because the structured note is unsuitable for Madam Tan. Although Madam Tan has previously invested in real estate, since retiring she has invested in fixed deposits and lower-risk energy utility stocks, and she now wishes to invest more of her portfolio in conservative equities. In addition, she shares that she is unsure what oil futures are or how they work. Under the guidance to III(C), members and candidates who are in an advisory relationship must consider carefully the needs, circumstances, and objectives of their clients when determining the appropriateness and suitability of a given investment, and must make reasonable efforts to balance their clients' trading requests with their responsibility to follow the agreed-on investment policy statement.

questions.stem: The ethical decision-making framework is most accurately described as:

options.A: A sequence of steps worked through in the order listed, ending when the member decides and acts.
options.B: An audit performed after a decision has been made, to detect violations.
options.C: A prospective aid for applying the Code and Standards, concluded by a review of the outcome.

rationales.A: The framework's components do not need to be addressed in a set order, and the process should not end at decide and act: a review of the outcome, the reflect step, should conclude it, and that review provides insights for improved decision making in the future.
rationales.B: The framework is a prospective aid for navigating ethical decisions as they are being made and for applying the Code and Standards. The concluding reflect step does improve future decision making, but the framework is not an after-the-fact compliance audit used to determine whether a violation occurred.
rationales.C: The framework is a useful framework to help navigate the ethical decision-making process and apply the Code and Standards. Its components do not need to be addressed in a set order, but a review of the outcome should conclude the process, and this review provides insights for improved decision making in the future. The four steps are: identify (relevant facts, stakeholders and duties owed, ethical principles, conflicts of interest); consider (situational influences, additional guidance, alternative actions); decide and act; and reflect (was the outcome as anticipated, and why or why not?).
